speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, even if I come very late, I should like to join all the previous speakers in offering my congratulations to the new Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) who has stepped into the shoes of men such as the

Supply-Transport
hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), the former hon. member for St. Antoine-West-mount and his predecessor, now heading the Department of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees).
Some of my colleagues in this house who do not belong to the same party as I do, often attack that man-I am embarrassed to see him here because I would have liked to say in his absence what I think of him. Some of my colleagues often attack the former minister of transport, now, the hon. member for Laurier, because he now represents a Quebec riding.
I find it really distressing that hon. members from my own province should make an exhibition of themselves in front of hon. members from the nine other provinces of this country, and wash their dirty linen in front of everybody, in this House of Commons.
The hon. member for Laurier associated his name with one of the largest Canadian undertakings, namely the St. Lawrence seaway. I am sure that that enterprise will have deep effects on the whole economy of our country, and, as a matter of fact those economic effects have already been felt in Canada.
Many years ago he started personal studies of the seaway project. He even sacrificed himself when the then prime minister of Canada, Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, asked him to accept the presidency of the seaway authority. It was a sacrifice for him, but at the same time he built something for his country.
I am sorry to see some of my colleagues who are trying to ruin his reputation by mean accusations. Their efforts are vain because we are standing by him and we will see to it that the people have a true knowledge of this man.
The present Minister of Transport also succeeded to one of my former bosses, Mr. Marler, who, I think, because I worked almost three years under him, did something for his country. He was not a politician, he was a businessman. He devoted all his heart, all his soul and all his intelligence to his country. He had a great intelligence and understood the problems of the nation.
The present incumbent of the office succeeded to the now Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I must say, without any intended reflection on his predecessor, that even though the present minister does not smile as easily, I am sure that he has the same devotion to

his office and the same sincere desire to discharge his duty. I wish to congratulate him and wish him well, and above all, I hope he will understand the problems faced by all ten provinces in this country.
In the next few minutes, I would like to bring to his attention some problems of my area. In doing so I am inspired more by love for my district than by my allegiance to my political party.
Some who came before me and who did not have my political convictions have already talked on behalf of what I want to ask the minister.
The hon. member for Chicoutimi suggested it long before me, and so did the mayor of Chicoutimi, I am referring to the dredging of the Saguenay river.
For four years, we have been trying to attract foreign industries. We are told that because of a lack of transportation, our situation is slightly unfavourable. Through the Department of Transport, I would like to spur the interest of the national harbours board in the Saguenay river.
We need new industries in our district. We need them because the heavy industries established in our parts had to lay off a number of employees due partly to a deterioration of our foreign market and partly to industrial automation. Those men have become experts and specialized labour, trained for heavy industry, the large industry, the electro-chemical industry. There is in our district a potential labour force which would like nothing better than to contribute to the development of the area while honourably earning their families' living.
I ask the Minister of Transport to examine that problem and not to take two or three years before putting in his estimates a vote for the dredging of the Saguenay river which, even though it does not flow through my riding, belongs to my district. I feel that a member when he is talking must forget about being re-elected and bear in mind above all the welfare of the whole district surrounding his constituency.
I am sure the hon. members for Lake St. John (Mr. Parizeau) and for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay) share that opinion and that one day they will speak out in this house, not because I advocated it nor because the hon. member for Chicoutimi advocated it, but because they love their region and want the common good of the community in which they live. The Lake St. John region is one of the most promising in Canada. Indeed, it has already done a great deal.

We have at Passe Dangereuse or Chute des Passes, a power station which generates one million horsepower. Shipshaw is one of the most productive power stations. We have the aluminum industry, the Price Brothers mills, the Consolidated Paper mills and the Lake St. John Paper mills in Dolbeau. The possibilities of that region are almost unlimited, if we would just help a little in the field of navigation.
The Minister of Transport is, I know, familiar with navigation, since he lives in Three Rivers. I do not have to tell him the importance of navigation on the development of a given district.
More than half of our population is under 21. That, I think, is exceptional. Our young people want to work. Every year, young people come out of technical schools and others, enter the abour market only to find that there are no opportunities for them. The government must show some interest in the matter and look after us; it could start by deepening the Saguenay river.
In another county there is another problem to which the hon. member for Chicoutimi has already referred: the St. Honore airport.
On several occasions, I have asked the minister's predecessor to try to do something in that connection.
The Department of Transport often states, and quite rightly, that it is interested in the development of civil aviation in Canada. According to the high officials and technicians of the department, the landing strips at that airport are in an exceptionally good condition considering the length of time the airport has not been used. At one time, I asked for a report on the matter. I know that the minister is extremely busy and that the administration of his department forces him to cover all sectors of the country's economy, but since I have received no report, I would like to know once and for all whether something definite could be done for the St. Honore airport and for the development of civil aviation in my area.
Investigations were carried out and the results were never made known to me. I do not usually speak like this in the house but I have been referring to this matter of the St. Honore airport for at least three years; my colleague from Chicoutimi is just as interested in the matter as I am, if not more so, and I would like the minister to see that his officials tell us definitely what they think of the whole matter and what the department can do about it.
There is another problem which is causing me concern just as it does to other members of my area, I am sure, namely the possible
Supply-Transport
combination of the C.N.R. express and freight services. In the past three or four months, I have met several employees who have heard of such a combination of services which, I am told, would be conductive to many lay-offs.
If the only people affected were those 24, 25, 28 or 30 years of age, I might understand the situation, but when the situation affects people who have worked 30 to 35 years for a public concern such as the C.N.R., who had a special training in a particular field, how can we expect those people to find employment elsewhere when for most of their life they have practised a trade which has no equivalent in other fields of private enterprise?
There is a human problem there that must be considered and I ask the Minister of Transport to take this up with the president of the C.N.R. I know, having worked in that department, that he might reply that the matter is entirely up to the C.N.R.; but I know of people who, when they used to sit on this side of the house, had rather bitter words for us about the whole problem of railway management. They are in power now. They are in-perhaps I should say they are "all in", Mr. Chairman, considering the way they act. They are in there, and if they remember what they said at the time they sat on this side of the house, if they are sincere, and I have no doubt they are, let them try their luck with the C.N.R.'s representatives and discuss, not only the economic problem, but also the human problem.
My colleague from Maisonneuve-Rose-mont (Mr. Deschatelets) referred to the Soulanges canal lands. First of all, I do not have all the facts relating to this Soulanges canal. I know one thing, however, and in this regard I leave out of consideration my political affiliation with those who are in Quebec city, but I know what they intend to do with the Soulanges canal, and the minister also knows, I am sure, because they have written to him. Besides, the minister of youth and the minister of game and fisheries have publicly stated the aims they would pursue if the province could acquire the Soulanges canal.
I am a little sorry that the member for Vaudreuil-Soulanges (Mr. Bourbonnais)-I did not know about it, it was my colleague from Maisonneuve-Rosemont who told me this afternoon-should have been the only one, according to the letter he published in a newspaper, to oppose the general welfare policy of the Quebec government.
When it is a question of our province, it seems to me that we could at least follow in

Supply-Transport
the footsteps of our colleagues from other parts of Canada who, whatever their political affiliation, always agree as regards the general welfare of their own province.
Whether we are Liberals, Conservatives, members of the C.C.F. group, or independents, whenever the common welfare of a province is at stake, we should forget our particular political allegiance. And, if the hon. member for Vaudreuil-Soulanges does not understand it, I hope that-even if he does not understand its platform-he will have enough regard for his own party to work for its re-election by favouring a policy which would benefit the citizens of our province. That is what I expect of those in authority, not only for my own province, but for every province in this country.
I want to say a few words about our merchant fleet. We heard so much about our merchant marine from the hon. gentleman who today heads the Department of External Affairs. When I was in the Department of Transport, I heard him make many a speech about our commercial fleet. He left almost nothing unsaid against the former ministers of transport with regard to our merchant navy.
One might have expected that, when the Conservatives would be in power, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs would be appointed minister of transport, so that he could practise what he had preached. But no, he was first appointed to public works, and then to external affairs. Moreover, instead of improving our shipping, they were satisfied to use the few remaining ships of the Canadian National Railways.
Recently, the Minister of Transport-and I must congratulate him for it-announced a new departmental policy on shipbuilding in Canada. However, two or three days afterwards, or even the very next day, the Minister of Veterans Affairs went on a trip to western Canada where, it seems, a byelection is going on, and said: "Our merchant marine is adequate to transport the wheat we sold to communist China."
But for over four years now the Conservatives have been managing the affairs of this country. And yet, that was one of the great promises made to Canadian voters. Today we are told: "We shall have a merchant marine when the need arises." Either they were sincere or naive when they were accusing us of having no merchant marine. I hope they were sincere. But, when I consider what happened in those four years I have my doubts about their naivete.
Before resuming my seat, I should like to suggest to the minister-and this will be doing him a service because there are so few

of us who think of helping him, poor man- that his department has become too important a body, affecting too many sectors of our economy, to be under the authority of only one man.
It is not that I do not find the present minister intelligent-and I am saying this seriously

but there is much talk about civil aviation and I think it is high time provision were made for a separate civil aviation division in the department. Or else let a new department be set up, if it is more agreeable to the minister, or perhaps Conservative members will have a more attractive suggestion. But let that department be divided. It is becoming too big; it affects too many sectors of our economy, for only one man to handle everything. I worked there for three months and I realized to what extent civil servants are devoted and competent in their field.
Besides, the minister must have realized this, since the time he has been there. At least I hope so. If he wants to prove to us he understands to what extent the Department of Transport is important to Canada, if he wants to give us concrete evidence that he understands that civil aviation is in constant development, and that the things of tomorrow are nearly those of today, I hope he will convince his colleagues of the cabinet that a department of civil aviation is imperative. It seems the minister just said a few words about that.

I lack that ability. But my colleague from Roberval (Mr. Tremblay) will accept it eagerly. Just the same, I rely on the minister, knowing that his officials are working so hard in the department. I have seen them at work and I have known them. If he fails to think of his men, we want to tell him about it. I hope he is working hard as a minister. Therefore, let him think of himself, and it will help him convince his colleagues in the cabinet.
I have been listening with close attention to my colleague from Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) who expressed certain grievances against the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. I am not aware of the facts he quoted to the house, but I can tell him one thing. I had occasion not too long ago to meet the directors of one of Canada's largest firms, and I well remember them asking me this question: "What do you think of this service?" I said: "I am no more in favour of socialism than you are, but what do you want? What are you doing to avoid it? You complain about having no say in the administration of your country or province, but what have you done to deserve it?"

I realize that a company director or president cannot be expected to resign from an industry to go into active politics. One thing I fail to understand, however, is that too many people are engaged in small private businesses and fail to realize that apart from active politics, they can have meetings with the people responsible for running the country or province. But they have no time for that; people often complain that they have no time for politics, but if they wait another five or ten years, many of those now in private enterprise will have no time for politics because they will all be civil servants.
Private enterprise must realize that it has a great part to play in the economy of our province and country. Gone are the days when politics could be left to anyone, to the demagogues or those who are motivated by one thing only: personal interest.
Mr. Chairman, I have been wandering a bit, but coming back to the point, I should like to remind the minister of the Saguenay waterway scheme. I hope he will look into it. I see he is smiling; I have confidence in his smile. I again urge him to consider my area.

I hope he will consider my area. In that way, he will be helping the economy generally. In considering other areas, he will be helping the economy of every province and of the country as a whole. That is my request to a man who is now vested with the authority of the Minister of Transport.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CHANGE IN SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
Before coming to the substance of my remarks I should like to pay a compliment to the Minister of Transport. I do not mean this as empty words. I believe sincerely that the minister has taken hold of this department and is giving it leadership which is second to none. He is a strong man, and he is worthy of all the compliments I can pay him. He may not get up and perform a lot of histrionics in the house but in the solid work of running a large department of government the hon. minister has few peers. While I am saying a few "thank you's" I should also say how grateful I am to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate for the gracious things he said last Wednesday.
I should like to talk about air lines, particularly. Many aspects of the work of this department are of importance to my province and to my area but the air lines is one of
Supp ly-Transport
the most important of the fields which concerns us. I should like to refer to the current annual statement of Trans-Canada Air Lines and to quote from this statement, not at length but here and there, in order to make a few points. On the first page it states:
Revenue growth started slowly reflecting the changed competitive situation. There was, however, marked acceleration in the latter half of the year under the stimulus of new equipment and lower Atlantic fares.
When you look at the table accompanying this statement you find that revenue from Atlantic fares did rise by 25 per cent but domestic revenue went up by 10 per cent also, which would appear to be a reasonably large increase. Checking over the balance sheet you find that capital commitments and contingent liabilities reflecting a balance of payment for equipment and construction amount to some $35 million. Of course, the fact that this air line has had a deficit for the first time in a good many years has been mentioned many times in this house. A deficit of some $2,600,000 has been mentioned but I have not yet heard anybody say anything with regard to the surplus. The balance sheet as of January I, I960, showed a surplus of $6,800,000, all of which disappeared this year. An explanation is given in a note on page 7 which says:
The surplus balance of $6,842,000 has been appropriated to establish a reserve against anticipated net differences between book value and the amount realized on the disposal of the piston engine fleets, their major components and supporting inventory.
Further on, the report points out that T.C.A. is the seventh largest air line in the world. As such, it should certainly be of a size to enable it to take advantage of the efficiency which comes from a large operation to operate at a profit. Perhaps we are paying a high price for the prestige of having the first all turbine fleet in the world. Perhaps we are paying a high price for forcing the obsolescence of aircraft such as 12 suDer constellations. All that surplus of 1960 disappeared because of the fact that these aircraft have not been in service long enough for the normal depreciation to take place to take care of the difference between their normal sale value and what the book value shows. This is where the surplus went.
I am also interested in looking at the timetable of T.C.A. overseas services. Under the T.C.A.-B.O.A.C. agreement are listed some 22 flights each way weekly over the Atlantic, 22 by T.C.A. and 22 by B.O.A.C. If you refer to the Aeronautics Act, part II, chapter 2, you will find, Mr. Chairman, that in section 15, subsection 7 it says:
The board shall upon application grant to Trans-Canada Air Lines a licence to operate a commercial

Supply-Transport
air service under such terms and subject to such conditions as will enable Trans-Canada Air Lines to perform any agreement made under sections 15 or 24 between the Minister of Transport and Trans-Canada Air Lines or between the Minister of Transport and any corporation created under section 19 of the act.
We have an anomaly here. We have an air transport board which is supposed to exercise control over air transportation in Canada, yet this board cannot control the operations of T.C.A. at the present time. Today the board is obliged to issue to T.C.A. without any hearing, public or otherwise, such licences as T.C.A. may require. Thus, in the absence of licensing power over T.C.A., the board is deprived of the normal controls relating to licensing which it exercises over all other scheduled carriers. The fact that T.C.A. services are covered by one licence means that T.C.A. can adapt and amend its schedules or flights in any pattern it wishes in order to cover those points. It is only when the company wishes to reach a new city or to extend to a location which it had not covered before that there is any vestige of control over this air line.
How does this affect other air lines? Other air lines have individual licences covering each route and they cannot make any changes without consent. For example, Canadian Pacific Air Lines has a licence to fly Vancou-ver-Edmonton-Amsterdam. Canadian Pacific Air Lines also has a licence to fly Vancouver-Penticton-Castlegar-Cranbrook-Calgary. But Canadian Pacific Air Lines cannot fly Van-couver-Calgary-Amsterdam because a licence to land and take off at Calgary is not part of the overseas licence issued to them. I contend that Trans-Canada Air Lines should have to show cause when they wish to fly over new routes. They should have to show that there is public necessity for such flights. The president of that air line said at a hearing in Ottawa some two years ago that he would be willing to fly his planes empty beside a competing carrier in order to drive that carrier out of business. This should not be possible.
We have a condition now where advertisements are appearing in Vancouver newspapers advertising flights by United States air lines to Europe. West coast people who wish to travel to Europe now fly by American air line because they can fly directly from Seattle to London which is the destination of most west coast passengers going overseas. Canadian Pacific Air Lines, one of our flag carriers, cannot do this. It cannot fly Vancouver-Edmonton-London. It must fly to Amsterdam, and then those passengers whose destination is London complete their journey on the K.L.M. system. Much of the traffic has been forced to United States air lines as a result of this situation. This situation has not helped

Trans-Canada Air Lines. If it had, why would there now be 22 flights a week across the Atlantic by B.O.A.C. and 22 flights by T.C.A.?
It seems all right to have this competition between air line carriers operating out of Toronto and Montreal to London, but it is not all right according to T.C.A. and the air transport board, that our own second flag carrier should operate from the west coast to London over a route which was pioneered by that company-I refer to the polar route- although T.C.A. announced some weeks ago that it intended to fly that route. I understand that T.C.A. did not have to apply for permission to do so because it was able to land at cities for which it already has licences. It just simply announced it was going to fly the polar route.
The government, through the former minister, as well as the present minister, announced that competition was to be controlled to the best interests of both carriers, but I suggest that competition is only controlled in regard to one; the other not being subject to the same control. The other carrier could make 50 flights per week if it wished to do so in order to give a frequency of service to drive its competition out of business even though this might result in a severe financial drain on the federal treasury.
I have in my hand a Trans-Canada Air Lines advertisement regarding trans-Canada and overseas flights. The paragraph appearing at the bottom of this advertisement reads as follows:
Also through jet flights from Vancouver, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Toronto, Cleveland and Halifax to Shannon, Glasgow and London.
The only sensible control on competition should have regard to regulations requiring air lines to plan their flights in such a way as to meet reasonable traffic demands, having regard to public convenience and economic considerations. The contention of hon. members from the west-I mean British Columbia when I say "the west"-has been that competing carriers should share in the growth of air line traffic, and not that one carrier should consider all growth to belong to it.
Trans-Canada Air Lines occupies a dominant position in eastern Canada passenger traffic and would, I suggest, still have 80 per cent of all traffic growth in the country, but the remaining 20 per cent increase, which exists generally in the west, represents a portion of passenger traffic in which C.P.A. should share.
I suggest the establishment of an all turbine fleet has involved a very high cost. This is particularly so because of the fact that 12 super constellations now sit in mothballs.

although they still had considerable service life. The lost from the sale of these 12 super constellations has undoubtedly accounted, in large part, for the elimination of the $6 million surplus which existed on January 1, 1960, but which does not exist today.
Mr. Chairman, I intend now to refer to the Wheatcroft report. I suggest it has reference to this department's estimates because it was following this report that the competition situation was opened for review.
Mr. Wheatcroft stated that the advantages of air line competition were: (a) more adequate service; (b) more efficient service; (c) more rapid technological progress; (d) more rapid traffic development; (e) a yardstick of efficiency, as no other method had yet been devised to achieve this as effectively as direct comparisons between competitive companies serving the same markets; and (f) the satisfaction of choice.
Hon. members who have travelled across the country by air will realize the drastic improvement which has been made during the last two years. I suggest that the travelling public has demanded this improvement, and has benefited from this competition. Mr. Wheatcroft also stated that the advantages of competition would be justified only if they did not involve a significant increase in the unit cost level of providing the air service. I think that is an important statement.
Mr. Wheatcroft pointed out, at the time of this report some two years ago, that the size of Trans-Canada Air Lines, at 270 million available ton miles per year, was well over the economy of scale size of about 150 million available ton miles per year. On the other hand, he observed that Canadian Pacific Air Lines, at 66 million available ton miles per year, was well below the level at which it could enjoy all the economies of large scale operations. The comparable figures for 1959, in this regard are, T.C.A., 357 million available ton miles per year, and C.P.A., 97 million available ton miles per year.
The figures I have mentioned, taken from Mr. Wheatcroft's report, bear out a statement made in the Trans-Canada Air Lines annual report, that it is now the seventh largest air carrier in the world. I suggest this is of great credit to previous governments, to the present government, and to the personnel of the air line itself. However, at the same time as this statement is made, the officials of Trans-Canada Air Lines profess concern because of the competition of one transcontinental flight per day by the second Canadian flag air line. Those officials are also worried about the result of allowing one Canadian flag carrier, out of approximately six air lines
Supply-Transport
flying from Canada to London, to land in that city. I should like to present a few examples of how this competitive air line is treated.
Canadian Pacific Air Lines flies a route from Vancouver to Mexico city, to Toronto and Montreal, but is not allowed to carry traffic between Toronto and Montreal. This is the same as Canada's treatment of foreign carriers. Canadian Pacific Air Lines is apparently subject to the same regulations which apply to foreign carriers. At one time, during the regime of the previous government, this company could not fly into Edmonton, but had to land at Yellowknife, making it more difficult for people to use this service. The present government has changed that situation and allows C.P.A. to land at Edmonton. However, a passenger, under present regulations, cannot travel from Vancouver to Edmonton by Canadian Pacific Air Lines, although that air line flies from Vancouver to Edmonton to Amsterdam. That is how Canadian Pacific Air Lines is being treated, as if it were a foreign and not a Canadian carrier. That air line should be able to fly Vancouver-Edmonton-Amsterdam and on other days Vancouver-Calgary-Amsterdam, and carry passengers between Canadian points.
On the other hand, Trans-Canada Air Lines is allowed to change its routes at will. I would suggest that if T.C.A. would devote half the effort which it is now putting into fighting this other Canadian air line toward improving its service and developing and extending their lines into the United States and tapping the markets which they have not yet tapped, it would be much better for both air lines.
Other members from British Columbia will have something to say on this subject. I am sure they will be touching other areas in addition to the areas I have covered in order to indicate that some changes must be made in the operations of the air transport board and of Trans-Canada Air Lines, which will make the board a functioning board and which will bring the government's own lines under the same rules and regulations that apply to other lines. This is the first essential. The second essential is that the private operator should not have to have this ridiculous dog's leg arrangement to Amsterdam and then through K.L.M. to London, but should fly there direct and thus stop feeding Canadian passengers to United States air lines because a Canadian air line cannot give the same service.
Canadian Pacific Air Lines is equally worthy of support, and equally worthy of commendation because of the job it has done in building up a rag-tag of routes around

Supply-Transport
the world, which were not wanted by T.C.A. and which in many instances they had to negotiate themselves, into an outstanding world air carrier.
I have heard that negotiations have been going on between T.C.A. and Japan Air Lines, in regard to onward passengers from within Canada going to Tokyo, whereby the government air line would direct traffic from C.P.A. to a foreign carrier, something like the B.O.A.C.-T.C.A. agreement. The same thing, of course, could be done with respect to Hawaii or any of the points reached at the present time by Canadian Pacific Air Lines.
The thing is, Mr. Chairman, these two companies must work in co-operation; they must work in the best interests of both companies, and this can only be done by government regulations. What hurts one is equally bad as what hurts the other. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I wish to say I am glad we have as head of the Department of Transport a minister who is willing to really get in and work on the problems which beset his department. I do hope that before too long he will be able to give some relief to a company which is a tremendous dollar earner for Canada, a tremendous producer of revenue from foreign lands, and which is one of the finest and best operations on the west coast, a company which has a major place in the over-all economy of the west coast.

Mr. Chairman, I would be remiss in failing to say a few words on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Transport.
A number of important and urgent projects of benefit to greater Montreal have been put forward by various members of the opposition, and particularly by the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Mai-sonneuve-Rosemont (Messrs. Chevrier and Deschatelets). I shall deal only with the more important ones.

The first one concerns the construction of a bridge in eastern Montreal. I think the minister recognizes the need, as this is an absolute must.
The second project is the use of C.N.R. land for the erection of east-west elevated highways.
The third concerns improvements to the port of Montreal, and particularly the development of a miniature park to allow local citizens and tourists to gain entrance to the port.
Those, Mr. Chairman, are urgent and necessary projects, of interest both to the federal government and to the Montreal authorities.
Mr. Chairman, apart from sitting in this house as member for St. Henry, I sit as member of the Montreal city council. I have often wondered what should be done to facilitate the implementation of those three schemes, which are so important for the economic development of Montreal.
In reply to a question I raised this morning concerning the erection of the elevated east-west highway, the Minister of Transport said he had received a brief from the city, about a month or five weeks ago. This was news to me.
I do not think such long distance discussions are a proper approach to our mutual problems. In that connection, I have a suggestion for the minister, and I hope he will give it serious consideration.
In dealing with such important schemes involving both the city of Montreal and the government at Ottawa, perhaps it might be helpful to set up a joint committee made up of a few city councillors and officials of the national harbours board, who could study the schemes and report to the minister.
I think this suggestion might facilitate and hasten the implementation of important works, if we want Montreal to remain the metropolis of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, first of all, along with other members, I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the minister on his appointment, not only because it is customary to do so but because I believe that in the time he has been minister he has already proved himself to be extremely capable. I know that his tenure of office is going to be a very valuable one to the transportation industry.
I want to say a few things tonight about transportation policy as it relates to labour relations. There will be some aspects of my remarks that, perhaps, will be of concern to the Minister of Labour as well, but I feel

they are more directly related to the field of transportation than they are to labour. I do not wish to rehash all the things that happened during the recent threatened railway strike. However, I believe that the positions that were taken by the various political parties at that time are of concern at the present time and will be more so in the future. This is one of those occasions when we have been able to get the opposition parties to state their policy and take a position with regard to it.
The committee will recall that when we were threatened with a strike the government took the position that collective bargaining should be the means of settling it and that they did not propose to offer any subsidy to cover wages. These were the two main statements that were made by the government. On the other hand, the position of the Liberal party has been quite clear for some time. When there was a railway strike in 1950, they imposed compulsory arbitration and advocated the same thing during the present situation. Then, we had the position taken by the C.C.F. party which advocated a subsidy to cover the wages of the railway employees. I thought that was a rather surprising position for that party to take because, over the years, they have always claimed that they were the spokesmen for labour in this country. I have never agreed with that view. I believe the actions they have taken in this regard prove substantially that they speak for special interests only. I would suggest they probably speak for those sections of organized labour which happen to contribute to funds for their party.
On other occasions when we have had protests made by unions, the C.C.F. group was very quick in bringing them to our attention. However, there was one protest that came from the employees of the trucking industry about which I have heard absolutely nothing from that party. While they were advocating a subsidy for wages of 111,000 railway employees, there were 90,000 employees in the trucking industry who were entirely opposed to such a policy. I think the action they took in recommending a subsidy for one segment of labour was a very wrong one.
I should like to bring to the attention of the committee a resolution that was passed by the Canadian conference of teamsters and sent to the Prime Minister. It reads as follows:
We, the undersigned truck drivers and employees of the trucking industry of the Dominion of Canada, are most violently opposed to past subsidies, and the proposed future subsidies granted to the Canadian railroads, which are to come out of public funds to the extent of better than six dollars per head. We therefore endorse the following resolution to be submitted to your government for immediate action:
Supply-Transport
Whereas: the Canadian government, over the past years has donated to the two Canadian railways, through subsidies, many millions of dollars out of the public treasury, and
Whereas: over the period of time during which the railroads have been receiving these millions of dollars, the same two railroads have been instituting non-profitable practices, such as: agreed charges on bulk commodities, at rates far below their operating costs, and piggy-backing at rates much lower than the recognized tariff rates, and
Whereas: both these practices place the trucking industry of the Dominion of Canada in an extremely difficult position, which will eventually eliminate many trucking companies, and
Whereas: through agreed charges, hundreds of truck drivers and trucking employees have been displaced, to further aggravate the unemployment situation, and
Whereas: during the past ten years, while the railroads have been receiving millions of dollars of public funds, the same railroads have been buying up truck lines to a point where they now control truck lines from coast to coast, at the expense of the public, and which, in a very short period of time, will result in a monopoly of the transportation industry such as existed before the trucking industry came into existence, and
Whereas: no other industry in the Dominion of Canada, under our private enterprise system of business, has been given the privilege of operating and paying dividends consistently from the public treasury.
Therefore be it resolved that the government of the Dominion of Canada cease the practice of making donations or subsidies to the Canadian railways, and be it
Further resolved that the government of the Dominion of Canada implement controlled minimum transportation rates and regulations which will allow all types of transportation a fair existence, to the common interest of the general public of the Dominion of Canada.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CHANGE IN SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
That
was not the position taken by the hon. member's party during the debates. I wanted to bring to the attention of the committee that when we consider a subsidy for wages, we must recognize that it is unfair to subsidize one group of employees when another group might well be affected.
Further, in relation to the labour question that has arisen and the positions that have been taken by the parties may I say this. The government has taken the position that collective bargaining should be allowed to take its course and that it should be the means of settling disputes. However, I should like to point out that the railroads have now gone very substantially into the trucking business. In fact, the Canadian Pacific Railway is the largest trucking organization in Canada and the Canadian National Railways operate the second largest trucking operation in Canada. The Canadian Pacific Railway has now started upon a course of integrating all of their trucking operations with their rail operations. They started this policy first of all in the province of British Columbia where

Supply-Transport
they were operating several truck lines. They were operating Canadian Pacific Transport, O.K. Valley Freight Lines, Island Freight Service and a number of others. They have decided to join those lines all into one organization known as Canadian Pacific Merchandise Services Limited and they have indicated their intention to pursue that policy all across Canada. All of their trucking operations will eventually be integrated into Canadian Pacific Merchandise Services and will comprise some 9,000 employees.
When this happened and this new organization was set up there, of course, had to be some bargaining agent for the employees of that organization. The teamsters' union went around and signed up a majority of the employees of Canadian Pacific Merchandise Services and applied for certification to the Canada labour relations board. The board told them that this was not an appropriate bargaining unit and that the people could not belong to the teamsters' union but must join one of the railroad brotherhoods even though some of the employees involved had previously belonged to the teamsters' union.
The point I wish to make in this regard is that if this policy is going to be pursued all across Canada, with the tremendous hold that the railways are getting upon the trucking industry it is going to mean that we are going to have all of our transportation services tied up under one union. If the government feels that we are to have collective bargaining I would suggest that the policy which should be followed is that those in the trucking industry should not be in the same union as those in the railroads, so that they would not all be tied up at the same time. I think that the Canada labour relations board were wrong in the decision they made at that time.
I have here a copy of the evidence that was taken at that time setting out clearly the intentions of the railroad. Not only do they intend to integrate all their services but they make it clear that they are out to compete with the trucking industry. I am quoting now from the evidence of Mr. Jacobson who was a witness for the Canadian Pacific Railway in the matter and I am referring to page 58 of the evidence before the Canada labour relations board on Wednesday, July 13, 1960. The chairman of the labour relations board had asked a question of Mr. Jacobson who was testifying. He asked this question:
Q. The purpose ot Canadian Pacific acquiring these subsidiary trucking lines was so that they would use the rail services or the road services according to how it might fit into the total picture: was that the purpose?
The answer given by Mr. Jacobson was:

A. Primarily the purpose was to engage in competition in the truck transporting industry over the highway-
That makes it clear that the railroads have set out on a policy to control the trucking industry and I believe that they have made substantial headway in that regard. As I have already pointed out, the C.P.R. is the largest trucking operator in Canada and the C.N.R. is the second largest one. I do not think that anybody in this country would wish to see the railroads get back into the monopoly position which they had for 100 years in this country. Every royal commission over the last number of years has come to the conclusion that the one factor that has helped in bringing down freight rates has been competition. If the alternative means of transportation are to be controlled by the railways, I suggest there cannot then be that degree of competition which otherwise would exist. I believe this is something that must command the immediate attention of the government because there really has not been any inquiry made into it. Trucking generally has been left in the hands of the provinces and there has really been no authority on the part of royal commissions to go to the lengths that are necessary in order to determine just exactly what the position is.
I have raised this matter on two or three occasions previously, but I believe it is far more serious now than it has been in the past, particularly when we relate it to the decisions that have been given by the Canada labour relations board so that we could have the whole of our transportation industry tied up. The MacPherson royal commission has pointed out that we would have had a very serious situation during the rail strike in 1950 if it had not been for the trucking industry. It becomes quite evident that if the trucking industry is now to be tied up at the same time as is the rail industry if a strike should occur, we would not be able to withstand it at all. The government would then not be able to follow this policy of allowing collective bargaining to take place because I am sure that the country would not be in a position to withstand a strike and the consequences of having all our means of transportation tied up. I would therefore ask the government to give very serious consideration both to policy and the Canada labour relations board. It may well be that the legislation under which that board operates will need to be changed in order to cover the situation. I ask the government to give very serious consideration to the acquisition of truck lines by the railways.
I wish to say a few words about transportation policy in general. I noticed that the hon. member for Laurier made a few comments the other day in which he set out a

rather detailed description of those things which had been done by the former administration. I do not want to go back as far over the whole history as the hon. member, but I do believe there are one or two things he perhaps overlooked which are of current importance and will be of importance in the future.
The hon. member for Laurier pointed out that the previous government had appointed the Turgeon royal commission in 1950 to investigate the problems connected with transportation and that a considerable amount of legislation was passed after the hearings of that royal commission in relation to the equalizing of freight rates in this country.
I suggest to the committee that the legislation the hon. member described to us as having been passed at that time did not solve the problem and could not have solved it because of the fact that the equalization had no effect on those rates which are known as competitive rates under the Railway Act.
These rates were set so that the railways could meet truck competition, be more flexible in their rates and set them very rapidly in order to meet this competition. That is, of course, as it should be and I am sure nobody in the country would want to see it any other way. However, it did mean that the board had no way of equalizing rates, because the railways were forced to reduce some rates where there was competition and they did not have to reduce rates where there was no competition.
One thing that arose from that legislation, as the hon. member for Laurier pointed out, was this. I refer to page 4879 of Hansard for May 16, where the hon. member is reported as having said:
Another feature of this legislation was the one and one third rule which is contained in section 337 of the Railway Act.
Of course, that one and one third rule means that on transcontinental freight where a rate is set, the rate cannot be more than one and one third times as much to an intermediate point. That fact alone indicates that there could not be equalization of rates if an intermediate point could carry a rate as much as one and one third times that of the ultimate destination.
However, even that was taken away in subsequent legislation because apparently the former administration was not as completely satisfied with the Turgeon report as the hon. member for Laurier indicated. The former administration appointed the Turgeon commission a second time, in 1954. At that time they were dealing with the question of agreed charges on railroads. It was a rather interesting situation, because the 1950 Turgeon commission was entirely opposed to agreed
S upp ly

Transport
charges on the railroads. I shall read one statement which is contained on page 92 of the report of 1951:
The point involves a question of whether the procedure should be simplified when the power granted to the railways is such an extraordinary one. The agreed charge method of rate making, even under the present practice, is contrary to well established principles of rate making under the Railway Act. It binds the shipper by agreement to ship all or an agreed portion of his goods by the carriers with whom he makes the agreement for a long period, usually for at least a year, and it gives the shipper a rate lower than the rate in the tariffs published under the Railway Act. This extraordinary procedure should be accompanied by the publicity and safeguards now required by the Transport Act. It must be remembered that the Railway Act now gives to the railways power to meet competition by the publication of competitive tariffs with a minimum of delay. The Transport Act adds to this power and empowers the railways to enter into agreed charges where the publication of competitive tariffs or special tariffs will not secure the object of the agreed charge. Such a power should not be exercised without close supervision. The procedure should not be simplified. It is important also that shippers and carriers should have an opportunity of being heard, so that the board may be made aware of all aspects of the question.
The report goes on to make a good many more remarks in that respect. However, I now want to come to the second Turgeon royal commission. The second royal commission inquiring into transportation dealt only with the application and effects of agreed charges. It held hearings in 1954 and reported in 1955.
This royal commission was brought about by a letter which the premier of Alberta wrote to the prime minister of Canada early in 1954. The letter stated, in effect, that through the application of agreed charges, Alberta was being deprived of the benefits of the one and one third rule which had been recommended in the 1951 royal commission report and which was incorporated in the Railway Act later that year. The government of Alberta had complained at the hearings of the first Turgeon royal commission, in 194950, about anomalies in the transcontinental competitive rates from central Canada to the Pacific coast as compared with the normal rates on the same traffic from central Canada to Calgary and Edmonton. The transcontinental competitive rates to Vancouver were made to meet the competition of steamships which operated through the Panama canal or direct to the Pacific coast ports.
The second royal commission came out very strongly in favour of agreed charges on the railways. That did away with the effect of the one and one third rule, because it was ruled subsequently that agreed charges were not covered by the one and one third rule,

Supply-Transport
so that rates in Alberta can be double or three times what they are to Vancouver in some instances.
That was one piece of legislation which certainly did nothing to equalize freight rates but actually considerably enlarged the discrimination. There is another bad feature of that legislation, in my opinion. This is that it did not require the railroads to be compensated for the cost of carrying goods under agreed charges.
The Railway Act states that the rate must be compensatory to the railroad; it must compensate them for at least their out-ofpocket costs. However, under the agreed charge legislation in the Transport Act there is no such stipulation; the railroads can set any rate they wish. An agreed charge is simply an agreement between the carrier and the shipper. I suggest this is unsound legislation because, as can already be seen, under the Railway Act the railways had sufficient power to meet competition from the trucking industry because they could set a competitive rate. If they were meeting competition from the trucking industry, they were able to set any rate they wished in order to meet that competition, provided it was compensatory to the railroad.
That is the main difference between the agreed charges under the Transport Act and the competitive rates under the Railway Act. I believe the government should take a very close look at the Transport Act for that reason. I am not going to go into that matter any more fully at this time, because I have already indicated my intention to proceed with a bill to amend that act, which I have placed on the order paper of the House of Commons.
However, the amendment in the bill I have placed on the order paper does not begin to cover the whole situation; it would only alleviate one aspect of it by making an appeal possible for the trucking industry. I think this is very little to ask, when the railroad has such extraordinary powers.
I also believe that having the power to set rates which are not compensatory may have influenced the railroads to set rates which are placing them in an even more difficult financial position than they otherwise would be. Certainly the rates on the railroads should be subject to examination by a competent authority.
At the present time, as I have indicated, the board of transport commissioners has no power over agreed charges. They simply receive them, file them and they automatically come into effect. There is a very limited appeal under the present legislation from the effects of that act, and in fact the people 
who would have a right of appeal under the legislation would be very unlikely to appeal because they are the people who would benefit from the low rates.
Unless an appeal is made and it is referred to the board of transport commissioners, they have no power to examine the rates to discover whether or not the railroad is being properly compensated for the goods they are hauling. A good deal has been said during the discussion in this committee, a great deal of it of a political nature, about freight rate increases over the years. I do not think we should get into a political hassle over which government was in power when freight rates were increased in the past. I think it is to be expected that there would be freight rate increases. Costs of every other description have gone up and I do not know why we should expect that rail rates should not have increased as well. However, the discriminatory effects of the increases are another matter. In order that the record may be clear in connection with what has happened by way of freight increases I wish to quote what the royal commission has had to say about that subject. They have been discussing the question of horizontal freight increases and on page 15 of their report they state:
There have been 12 such increases, including interims, approved since 1948 which has resulted in a permitted level of increase amounting to 157 per cent. However, even abstracting the effect of statutory rates, the consequences of the competitive situation are revealed by the fact that with this permitted amount of increase in rates the railways had only been able, by the end of 1958, to obtain an increase in average revenues per ton mile of less than 55 per cent.
I think some of the statements about freight rate increases which have been put on record have been very misleading. I say they have been misleading regardless of which party was in power, because I do not believe the government has all that much control over freight rate increases. Wages and costs of every description have been rising and I believe it is only to be expected that freight costs should increase. I am sure they have gone up in other countries just as they have gone up here.
Then, again, there was another statement which the royal commission had to make on page 12 which, I think, puts the position of our freight rates into better perspective. Here again they have been talking about freight rate increases and on page 12 the commission is reported as stating:
In this connection it is of interest to note that notwithstanding its recent rapid growth the cost of the transportation function relative to the gross national product appears to have declined from about 8J per cent in 1946 to something in the order of 61 per cent in 1959.

This is not to say we have no problem in connection with freight rates in this country but I believe this quotation puts the position in better perspective.
The question has been asked by some members of the opposition why the government has not rushed to implement some of the recommendations of the MacPherson royal commission. First of all, the suggestion was made that the government had had the report for months but was doing nothing about it. Then it turned out that at the time the statement was made the report had been in the hands of the minister for less than a month. However, there is a statement contained in the report itself which I think advances convincing ground for not rushing in to implement some of the recommendations which are contained in the first volume of the report.
I drew to the attention of this house the other day that this was only the first volume of the complete report and that I thought it would be precipitate to rush in and implement the first proposals we came across. This is a statement which the commission itself makes in the preface to the report:
Volume II *will, among other things, examine these particular problems. To say that they are less vital than those dealt with in volume I would be to understate their importance. The growing intensity of these special problems-local, regional or industrial in nature-is, as we are well aware, immediately responsible for the appointment of this commission. However, we feel strongly that we are in a better position to treat them now that our analysis in volume I has given us insight into the structural nature of the transportation foundation upon which they rest.
So the royal commission itself feels that the first volume is a broad study of the whole transportation picture and that the question which led immediately to the setting up of the commission has not even been dealt with in the first report. I think any criticism of the government for not proceeding immediately to implement the recommendations of this report is completely unwarranted. The commission goes on to state that further recommendations will not be long delayed. I hope this will be the case because there are many important problems which still have to be dealt with. I am sure the present minister is well aware of the situation, as he has clearly indicated by the actions he has already taken, and that he intends to take those steps which are necessary to correct the difficulties we are experiencing in transportation at the present time.
One of the matters which the hon. member for Laurier brought to our attention concerned some of the subsidies which had been paid under the previous administration. The hon. gentleman felt that these were the results of good pieces of legislation, and no
Supply-Transport
doubt they helped to some extent to relieve inequities at the time they were passed. However, as a long term transportation policy I do not believe they were good. I have stated in the committee now that I do not believe embarking on a long term policy of subsidization is the proper course to follow. I think this is recognized by the MacPherson royal commission report, even though the commission recommends further subsidies for a limited period of time. I think one of the things which the commission itself has not fully recognized is that once subsidies are paid it is difficult to stop them, irrespective of any recommendation that they should be paid for one or two years only. This is true of the subsidy we are now paying under the Freight Rates Reduction Act. We were told at the time it was going to be for a year only, but we have had to extend that period on two occasions. I use that example by way of illustration.
I should like to quote what the royal commission had to say on page 21 of this report with regard to previous subsidies. The commission is speaking about subsidies which have been paid in the past, and it says:
Measures such as these, while they help to alleviate freight rate inequities cannot by themselves solve the underlying problems. Moreover, in the form in which they have been applied they may tend to distort the competitive market in transportation with resultant adverse effects upon the transportation system as a whole.
I think that is a clear-cut indication by the commission that even though subsidies are recommended in this instance they feel strongly that a policy of subsidization should not be entered upon as a long term policy but should be strictly curtailed and should only be sufficient to compensate the railroads for services they are obliged to carry on even though those services might not be economic.
As far as the latter subsidies are concerned, I am surprised that the commission should have recommended them. It is, of course, to be realized that the Canadian Pacific Railway is a private company. It has not lost any money, and it does not seem to me that the government should be paying a subsidy to a private company which is not even losing any money, particularly when the commission has recommended that the company be allowed to curtail some of the uneconomic services which it has been operating. The commission has recommended, with a sense of urgency, that the company should abandon these unprofitable operations but it seems to me that the payment of a subsidy in these circumstances could do nothing but destroy this sense of urgency. Obviously, if a subsidy is paid for carrying them on there will be so

Supply-Transport
much less desire on. the part of the railroads to discontinue these branch lines particularly when there are pressures throughout the country in favour of their retention.

I am
grateful to the committee for this opportunity to conclude my remarks. I assure hon. members I shall not be too long.
May I add that I realize there are a lot of social implications attached to the measures which have been suggested, in particular to the proposal that the railways should curtail their uneconomic passenger operations and curtail the operation of branch lines which are uneconomic. I believe this presents a serious problem and one which must be given careful study. I know that across the prairie provinces, particularly, farmers have depended for a good many years on these branch lines. Of course, they have the benefit of the Crowsnest pass rates for their grain. The result of tearing up these branch lines would be an additional cost to the shipper in transporting his grain to a rail centre. I feel we should consider whether it is costing more to keep these rail lines in operation, than perhaps it would cost to provide some other form of compensation, or would cost to provide alternative transportation facilities for the moving of grain to rail centres.
The hon. member for Assiniboia asked, a day or two ago, for assurance that the government would not advocate a policy of tearing up these branch lines on a wholesale basis. I think that assurance is unnecessary because the royal commission has not even hinted at such a procedure. The commission report has recommended that alternative transportation systems are to be made available in the case of the abandonment of a branch line, and I am sure the government will not rush into any such wholesale project.
Regarding the loss suffered by the railways in the provision of passenger service, I suggest this is a field from which the government of Canada should encourage the railways to depart as quickly as possible, particularly when alternative transportation systems are available which are comparable and sometimes even lower in cost.
When I was attending the United Nations session at New York a short time ago my wife made arrangements to return home, and found that it was cheaper for her to do so
[Mr. Browne (Vancouver-Kinsgway) .1
by air than by rail. If that situation persists generally, particularly in view of the fact that bus transportation has progressed to its present fast, efficient and inexpensive service, there certainly is no necessity for carrying ol this uneconomic railway passenger service.
Last year the railways lost approximately $65 million in providing this service, as a result of which the government is being asked to provide a subsidy to offset the loss. The money to be provided as subsidy to the railways must come out of the taxpayer's pocket and I am sure the taxpayer will not be happy to continue on this basis unless it is absolutely essential. I suggest that it is not essential to do so, in view of the other efficient and economical forms of transportation that are available.
I feel the government should consider this aspect, and the recommendations contained in the royal commission report in respect of it, at once. I do not believe our railways should be allowed to continue these uneconomic operations. I do not refer, of course, to the essential commuter services which are provided for individuals who must necessarily travel back and forth to work, but I do not believe that is an uneconomic service.
The railways have made many applications to the board of transport commissioners to discontinue some of these operations but have been refused throughout the years. However, I feel that these services will eventually have to be done away with. I suggest that if we must continue to subsidize them, it would be far better for the railways to withdraw this type of service on an orderly basis, particularly where there is another satisfactory means of transportation available. I think it would be wise to initiate an orderly program of withdrawing these uneconomic services provided by the railways in an attempt to place the railways in a position where they can support themselves without subsidies. If we do not do this, we will surely arrive at the point where we cannot subsidize them any longer, and the financial structure of the railways will collapse. I have no doubt that this will eventually happen, if we continue with our present program, ending each year with a deficit, as did the C.N.R. last year, amounting to approximately $65 million. I do not believe these services should be continued on that basis, and suggest that the government should consider all of the social implications and recommendations of this royal commission report. The government will, of course, wish to consider the contents of the two volumes of the report yet to come, before entering into any long term program such as I have suggested.

Mr. Chairman, I have drawn these facts to the attention of the minister, and the government, and I hope that consideration will be given to them at this time.

The Minister of Transport, on the one hand, asserts that the waterway would not be economic, while on the other hand, every engineer and town planner and expert in the field, both in Canada and the U.S., says the scheme would be economic.

It is about time Canada and the United States made a joint study of the Richelieu waterway scheme.

Since 1958, according to the report of the Canada-U.S. joint commission-which incidentally is made up of reliable people- Canada should have been studying the problem of the Richelieu waterway. I should like to speak for a minute or two on this particular item. My main concern is, perhaps, with the Canadian National and its operations. The Canadian National operates numerous branch lines in my constituency. I am well aware of the causes for laying off men from railways such as dieselization, the centralization of car shops and repair shops, the advent of the steel wheel, roller bearings, steel box cars and so on.
The thing which concerns me particularly, and concerns my constituents, is this new regional set-up with regard to management. There are five vice presidents and each vice president is to manage his regional area. This may well result in an improvement in the management of the Canadian National. It may speed up railway operations and make the railways more competitive. However, there is a great fear among railway workers that railway operations are becoming top heavy, that we are getting fewer and fewer workingmen and more and more administrators. Then, too, costs go up to a greater extent with additional superintendents and vice presidents. In this connection, I am thinking particularly of expense accounts. Certainly, some of the vice presidents can run up large expense accounts. We have never had any figures given to us to indicate what the total of these expense accounts would be which are run up by the various managers and vice presidents of the Canadian National.
Another thing that concerns me is the lengthening of the sections and reduction in the number of section men across Canada. I can well understand that dieselization would bring about a reduction in car repair shops but why should it bring about a reduction in the number of section men and the lengthening of sections, particularly when there is no improvement to the track in those various areas? Does this procedure cause more accidents on the railway line? We are certainly all well aware of a number of accidents over the past years that have been brought about for one reason or another. Could those accidents have been prevented if the section crews had not been reduced in some areas?
Another matter about which I have been wondering is whether the increased amount of advertising has paid off. We are now spending in the C.N.R. approximately $2 million

on advertising alone. Has the deferred payment plan for passengers increased revenue derived from passengers? Hon. members may think that these questions could be well asked in the sessional committee which deals with the C.N.R. However, may I say that I have not been fortunate enough to become a member of that committee, as far as I know, and I am therefore putting these questions forward.
This afternoon I noticed that the hon. member for Vancouver East made a speech with regard to C.N.R. operations and how irritating conditions were for a passenger travelling on the C.N.R. trains. I must say that I have noticed things similar to what he mentioned. I note that these things were brought to Mr. Gordon's attention in the report of 1959 by the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose. He dealt with them at length at page 81 of the minutes and proceedings and evidence of the committee. He told Mr. Gordon that he should have somebody make some inquiry into these conditions with regard to passenger service on the trains, and mentioned instances of persons having boarded and found the coaches practically empty in some cases but yet it was difficult to get a reservation on a particular line. Mr. Gordon as much as told him at that time that these conditions did not exist and that, if they did exist, he did not know about it; and he as much as said that he was not going to do very much about it if they did exist.
The hon. member for Vancouver East went on to speak about the sham battles that take place, and are becoming more and more evident day by day, between the railways buying up trucking firms and so on. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, as will be found in the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the 1960 committee, made a motion to the effect that these figures be given and that no money be appropriated for the C.N.R. in order to further these expenditures for trucking interests. This can be found at page 221 of the proceedings of the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping. But what did the hon. member for Port Arthur say at that particular time? I am reading from the third paragraph on page 221. He said:
I would like, if I may, to speak against Mr. Browne's motion.
Then he goes on to state some of his reasons. However, the point I wish to raise here is this. Two days ago the hon. member for Port Arthur got down on his knees, figuratively speaking, and pleaded with the members of the House of Commons that they help him in the sessional committee this year to get facts

and figures on the operations of the Canadian National Railways. Here was a specific motion made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway with regard to facts and figures on the operations of the C.N.R. What did the hon. member for Port Arthur do? He rose and spoke against the motion. Yet he has the gall to rise in his place here in the house and plead with us to help him to get facts and figures. It was purely a publicity speech for his own purposes designed to enhance his personal prestige in his own constituency. He made no real attempt in the committee at various times to promote the ideas in which he professes interest.
Hon. members know that this is not the only time this situation has arisen. Going back to the committee of 1959, I find that a similar situation arose when the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., wanted information with regard to the Victoria harbour and the docks there. He suggested that this information be given to the committee as found at page 197 of the 1959 report. Various members spoke for and against the motion. I looked for the name of the hon. member for Port Arthur in order to find whether he had said anything about the motion. Here is more evidence as to whether or not he wanted facts and figures at that particular time. I went from page 197 to page 208 and as found at page 208 the hon. member for Port Arthur said, "I do not like that motion". Then as found at page 209 he went on to speak with regard to another subject. Here again is evidence of the sincerity of his approach in pleading with the members of the House of Commons to support him allegedly the lone person asking for facts and figures in regard to the operations of the C.N.R.
Another instance arose. The hon. member for Vancouver South will likely remember it better than I do. It was with regard to R.C.A. Victor and their transmitting facilities on the C.N.R. I have not had the time to look up the exact quotation with regard to the hon. member for Port Arthur. At that time he did not support the hon. member for Vancouver South in the motion with regard to facts and figures on that particular aspect of the operations of the C.N.R. Yet he pleads with members of this House of Commons to support him in getting the facts and figures on the operations of the railway.
I have read through the remarks made by the hon. member for Port Arthur in the last two years with regard to the operations of the C.N.R. He has been greatly concerned with the personnel and I agree with a great many things he has said with regard to the operation of the C.N.R. in the matter of hiring of personnel and lay-offs. I know how this matter concerns men working on the

railway. However, I fail to find in the last two years any instance where the hon. member for Port Arthur had asked for facts and figures. Here was the closest instance I could find. It is found at page 94 of the 1959 committee report. He said this:
I am not asking for them, but I wonder if you have figures which would indicate the number of revenue passengers you need, say between Montreal and Vancouver to make the Super a paying proposition?
Then Mr. Gordon said this:
I do not have them with me. They could be secured.

I do not want them.
This sort of thing occurred time and again. He made no real inquiry into the facts and figures with regard to the operation of the C.N.R. He was concerned about the personnel. In this matter I agree with him and I share his concern as to the reduction of employees of the C.N.R. I have a number of C.N.R. employees in my constituency. I find that they are more concerned about their jobs on the railway than they are about anything else. They are more concerned about their jobs than they are perhaps even about pay increases. I think that the committee inquiring into the C.N.R. this year, when it begins to function, should concern itself more with the actual prospects of the C.N.R. and their operations, whether or not these operations are a paying proposition, and that it should obtain facts and figures as to whether or not it was profitable for C.N.R. to sell certain various hotels or to lease other hotels, and that it should get down to the actual operations of the railway and tie that information in with the men that are employed on the C.N.R.
But when we consider the new party's approach to the C.N.R. and its whole operation, they suggest, "Take over the C.P.R. too". I do not know how this would improve or enhance the railway workers' jobs. I do not know how it would bring greater stability among railway workers, and I think this is their primary concern today.
To my mind it would bring about a greater amalgamation of the two railways and the firing of a greater number of employees, because in certain passenger lines, particularly transcontinental lines, one might be dropped and the other continued. This would have the effect of reducing the number of men employed by the C.N.R.
Not very long ago the hon. member for Port Arthur suggested to this house that Donald Gordon should be fired. He put it as plainly as that and said it three or four times. I am not going to lead the committee into thinking that I disagree with him on this particular point, because I do not. I

have studied the hon. member's remarks, and without doubt he has a great deal of information and knowledge in regard to the operations of the C.N.R., but I think he has been a secret admirer of Donald Gordon for a number of years.
I should like to refer to the famous Donald Gordon statement which is to be found in the 1959 committee report. I am sure most hon. members have heard it by now and are well aware of it. I refer to Donald Gordon's remarks when it was suggested he should be fired:
-the management of the C.N.R. an efficient management, or otherwise: and if you come to the conclusion it is not, for God's sake tell us and fire the lot of us.
When he suggested this, the hon. member for Port Arthur did not immediately say, "Yes, we should fire you" or anything of the kind. He was rather silent. He made one short remark after that, "That is up to the House of Commons to decide", or something like that. But at no time, to my knowledge, in the three cases I have cited, has the hon. member ever gone against the wishes of Mr. Gordon in supporting the motions that were moved with regard to the trucking industry, the harbour at Victoria or the transmitting services of R.C.A. Victor.
Therefore I question this idea of his to fire Donald Gordon. I think it is one he gathered just recently when he was back home among the railway men and they told him that Donald Gordon was pretty unpopular. I think he grasped the idea and perhaps said, "I will see that he is fired", or, "I will try to have him fired; I will suggest it to the House of Commons". It would be a mighty popular suggestion to his people back home, and this is no doubt why he said it.
