I do not want to deal with the recommendations made in the royal commission's report at this time. They have been talked about enough. I will not refer to them now, particularly as the first volume is the only one that is out as yet. But as for this idea of the C.P.R. being taken over by the government, I cannot see how this would improve the government's or the workers' position. It may cut down transportation costs by a small amount, or a great amount; I do not know. Apparently none of the royal commissions which have studied transportation costs have been able to figure out what they are. Nobody has been able to arrive at a concrete answer as to a great many of the cost problems in railroading. Therefore I think it would be hard to prove that by taking over the C.P.R. we would actually be cutting down

Supply-Transport
transportation or freight costs by a great amount. But we would certainly be weakening the position of the men now working on the railroads. We would bring about chaos within their ranks with regard to holding a job and seeking employment in general.
My own view is that the C.N.R. is much like the operation of a hockey team or a ball team. The morale is mighty low. I am sure all hon. members have travelled on the C.N.R. and have found that the morale of the people working on the C.N.R. is low. I know that whenever a team's morale is low they are not going to win very many games. There is one thing that always enhances the morale of a team, and we see this done often in football and baseball. They are always firing coaches to improve the morale and get the winning spirit back in the team.
I think this applies to the C.N.R. We must fire the coach to improve the morale of the team. This would bring about a greater improvement in the deficit figure and in the revenue of the C.N.R. than anything I can think of right now. Firing the coach would bring about a greater improvement because the morale would immediately be boosted and the workmen's efficiency might improve. To some extent I agree with the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose and the hon. member for Vancouver East, that there is room for improvement in the efficiency of operations in the C.N.R. and the total efficiency of the workers. As I have mentioned, the morale is low, and I think by firing the coach the morale would immediately pick up.
I also have one more thought that I might just as well leave with the committee. It is with regard to the coach's salary. We are now splitting up the administration of the C.N.R. into five regions, as I understand it. Five vice presidents are going to have managerial control over their particular regions. They are going to have control as to setting the rates in each region and as to getting out and seeking freight to haul in those regions.
Therefore those vice presidents are going to carry a greater load of the responsibility in the operations of the C.N.R. To my reasoning this will automatically reduce the work and the responsibility of the president of the C.N.R. Therefore I think-and I recommend this to the committee-that the salary should be cut in half and that a new coach should be hired.

speechtext:
Excuse me, Mr. Chairman; it is Kootenay West. Apparently you, sir, have the idea that I am going to speak on a favourite topic.
After the torrent of words uttered by the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napier-ville my effort this evening will appear like a slow-flowing, babbling brook. After listening to the hon. member for Acadia, with his lion-like form of eloquence, I shall appear like a lisping infant.
Mr. Chairman, I rise to briefly mention one matter that is of some concern to myself and a number of other persons who are interested in the prevention of pollution of our lakes, springs, rivers and waters generally. I rise because I have a particular and personal knowledge of the pollution of some of our smaller streams and lakes in British Columbia, as the result of mining companies being permitted to dump tailings into them. This has in a very short time destroyed fish life, spoiled the water for drinking purposes and so lessened the value of the area that persons no longer wish to boat on these streams and lakes. Crystal-like sheets of water have been changed into turgid, and in many cases, slimy sheets of water. So far the pollution has been on a limited scale, and in recent years the government of British Columbia has taken action to prevent the continuation of this vandalism by making it obligatory for mining companies to install settling ponds; they are no longer allowed to dump their tailings except in special circumstances in very deep water.

I was interested in a proclamation announced in the January 25 edition of the Canada Gazette Part II, volume 95 under the heading "Navigable Waters Protection Act-Proclaiming Water Lot in Labrador Exempt from Section 20 of the Act." I shall read just a section of this proclamation which gives me great concern.
Whereas in and by section 22 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, chapter 193 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, it is provided that our governor in council may, from time to time, by proclamation, declare any navigable rivers, streams or waters or part or parts thereof, exempted, in whole or in part, from the operation of those sections of the said act which prohibit the deposit of rubbish or other material in navigable waters,
And whereas an application has been made by the Labrador Mining and Exploration Company Limited for exemption from the operation of section 20 of the said act of a water lot being all and singular that piece of land covered by the waters of Wabush lake in the electoral district of Labrador North described as follows-
I am not going to read out the description of this land. The proclamation continues:
And whereas it is expedient and our governor in council has advised that a proclamation do issue declaring that the area described above be exempt from the operation of section 20 of the said act.
Now know ye that we, by and with the advice of our privy council for Canada, do by this our proclamation declare the area described above exempt from the operation of section 20 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act as aforesaid.
I raise the matter on these estimates because I understand there is a dual responsibility with respect to the administration of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, shared by the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport. It may be that special circumstances do justify this exemption under section 22 of the act, but I am raising this matter because I think all Canadians and especially members of this committee should be completely aware of what may lie ahead if our waters are allowed to be further polluted.
I wish to ask the minister a series of questions. Where is Wabush lake which is mentioned in this announcement? What is its size? Was the Department of Fisheries consulted before exemption was given under section 22 of the act and this company was given permission to pollute this water by dumping its mining tailings into the lake? Would the minister mind telling the committee the character of the residue in the mining tailings, whether they are of an acid type or not? Will this pollution of the water in accordance with the permission given destroy the fish in this lake, and will it destroy the possibility of the development of this lake for recreational purposes? Is it sufficiently close to ordinary transportation 90205-6-318

facilities to be developed in the near years ahead for recreational purposes? I should like the minister to explain the reason why this exemption was given, because I think this is a matter of importance, particularly in view of the increasing interest of Canadians in the pollution problem with respect to our waters and the growing demand for the protection of the fresh water we have left in this country.

speechtext:
Along with other members I should like first of all to congratulate the Minister of Transport on the fine work he has been doing. I do not know whether or not he is tired of hearing this, but his department and the hon. gentleman himself have been very co-operative and have helped me in a great many ways, so I am pleased to have this opportunity of thanking them.
The Department of Transport is one of the most important departments of our government, and presents perhaps the greatest challenge of our times to the people of Canada. Air transport in the world today is ever changing and Canada is just on the doorstep of the great things to come in this new age, the age of jet transportation.
Heavy jet aircraft introduced during 195960 have stepped up the pace of aviation and the jet aircraft to come will be larger and heavier than ever in the near future. The large aircraft manufacturers are spending millions of dollars on research; their designers are working on their drawing boards; their engineers are building models and testing them in their wind tunnels, and it is very necessary that countries that want to be part of the great future in air travel keep abreast of these advancements.
Until a few years ago, an air crash did not take nearly the toll of human life that it does with the new jets of today carrying over 100 passengers, and the jets to come will carry many more than today's air liners. The Department of Transport have their part to play in the matter of safe air travel and it does not stop with the inspection of aircraft. It should be the duty of the Department of Transport to build and maintain our airports and runways. These runways must be properly built for the new age, they must be wider, longer and more strongly constructed.
The terminal airports of our trans-continental and trans-ocean air lines which will use these future giant jets should be reserved exclusively for the use of these large aircraft. Feeder line aircraft should use another runway. The large jets should be able to make a direct approach, not a circuitous approach, as some of the air disasters have been caused by fast aircraft making a circuit while they have waited for a clearance from the control tower.

Supply-Transport
In the future, all aircraft other than transcontinental should have their own runway adjacent to the trans-world, or jet runway, and it is my thought that the Department of Transport should plan along these lines and start at once with their planning.
This age is indeed a challenge to Canada, but Canadians have met many challenges since the days of confederation and will meet many more. In the history of aviation, Canada and Canadians have been second to none. When we think back to the days of world war I, and the record that Canada achieved both in the building of aircraft and the training of airmen; when we remember the great Canadian bush pilots and the building of civilian air lines, we know that Canadians will always be in the van in the future development of our air transportation.
Mr. Chairman, in the early days I flew aircraft in Canada when there were no airports. We used fairgrounds. In those days there were no landing lights, and there were no rules or laws to be broken. We flew at night without running lights, and without landing lights. It is interesting for me to think back on those early days of flying. I remember that at one time in the city of Victoria we were trying to get permission to use a fairground for flying. One of the aider-men got up and said he was very much opposed to granting permission to any of what he called these infernal contraptions flying around. The aeroplane, in his opinion, was certainly not here to stay, and he was very much opposed to granting permission. However, there happened to be two or three younger men on the city council and finally they gave us permission to go ahead and put in an air field. It must be remembered we had no landing lights and no running lights; we had no radio to guide us, and once we were in the air we were on our own. We could fly at any time in those days. There were no regulations laid down by the Department of Transport covering this type of flying as there are now. We were all freelance flyers then and could fly at night if we were foolish enough to do so.
I remember in 1923 I was commissioned to fly a flying boat to Seattle to meet the President Jefferson liner from the Orient, to pick up pictures of the Japanese earthquake, and fly them to the Illustrated News of Los Angeles. I did not get very far. I had two passengers with me when I left the harbour some time after midnight, but unfortunately when we got airborne we developed motor trouble and had to land again. I always felt it was a log that we hit when landing, but it could have been anything. We turned over

two or three times and ended up neck deep in water, and stayed that way until assistance arrived.
I have recounted this story to give hon. members an idea of the very fine and necessary work the Department of Transport has done in this field since the early days. With today's existing regulations we cannot get into that kind of trouble. I should perhaps also mention that we did not have to get clearance from Seattle, Washington, nor clearance when we arrived in Victoria, British Columbia. When we did finally pull the plane up, officials from the department of immigration arrived as well as officials from the customs branch, and it is very interesting to remember that those officials did not know how we should be entered in their reports, or what classification applied. Today all these details have been taken care of through the application of the many regulations and rules. I would suggest the implementation of these regulations by the Department of Transport had a good deal to do with the development of air transportation.
In those early days of barnstorming, pilots had to sell the idea of flying to their potential passengers. I am sure this spirit of competition had a lot to do with the building up and developing of present day air line services. I suggest that feeling of competition is still valuable and will be of value in the future to the improvement of air transportation facilities. I can well remember the airports of the early days. They were nothing compared to airport facilities of today. In those days, if a flying service had five or six planes lined up in a row, that service secured the major portion of the air traffic. Individuals would perhaps make ten week-end visits to the airfield and talk to three or four different pilots before finally being convinced that they should go for a ride. The pilot who had the best sales pitch was the one who acquired the business. A ten minute trip in those days cost $15. There was no jealousy between the pilots and the operators of the flying services because they felt the pilot who secured business in this field was doing his duty to convince people that this was a safe and good way to travel, and this type of salesmanship was responsible for the development of a great deal of interest in flying.
I believe our air lines are today on the doorstep of a tremendous advance in the transportation system, and I feel we should have two major air lines in Canada because with the proper development of this business one air line eventually will not be able to handle the traffic. I understand that Trans-Canada Air Lines are now accepting first

class transportation only. I feel that the Canadian Pacific Air Lines under the able leadership of Grant McConachie, who is one of our pioneer flyers who did a tremendous job for Canada in creating interest in this field of transportation, should be licensed to operate flights to London. If this air line used propeller type aircraft, such as the Britannia, many people would be able to afford to fly to London and return who are not at present day prices able to do so. I feel this would be a step forward in the development of the Canadian air transportation industry.
There are many people today who do not even consider making such an air trip because they feel the cost, in addition to the expenses of living ten days in a city such as London-visiting all the places and seeing all the things they should see there-is more than they are able to afford. However, with the provision of a cheaper service, such as I have suggested, I feel there would be an increase in air traffic. I would suggest that without this service provided by Canadian air lines, this potential increase in air passengers will be taken by foreign air lines. I am sure that Canadian Pacific Air Lines, which has always been a pioneer in this field, would do a marvellous job in this respect. When one considers the potential development which could take place in this direction and the benefits our air line services could derive in this regard one must come to the conclusion that this is a worth-while step to be taken.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make it very clear that I believe Canadian Pacific Air Lines should be given the privilege of operating flights to and from London. I firmly believe there should be two large Canadian air lines operating with equal rights and licences both in Canada and international areas. I believe that competition in this field is necessary to the development of Canada's air transportation system so that it will continue to be considered among the best in the world.
I should offer as a further reason for the expansion of our air transportation system particularly in Canada, the necessity of having completely Canadian controlled air transportation facilities in the event of another war. I am not suggesting that war is an in-evitibility, but I do suggest that during these days of continuous threat from foreign powers, we must build up our transportation system by increasing our facilities, and training more and more pilots. With two major Canadian air lines, many of these developments would take place normally.
Turning now to the situation regarding the Nanaimo airport-and I have drawn this to 90205-6-318J
Supply-Transport
the minister's attention on other occasions- it is essential that the landing strips be lengthened. There is plenty of land available to the Department of Transport to do this. With the advent of jet cargo planes, both for defence and commercial use, it is very necessary that this work be commenced as soon as possible. The coast route to Alaska could be serviced from the Nanaimo airport. The Pacific route to the Orient could also be served from the Nanaimo airport, and transcontinental runs could originate from that same airport. In view of the fact that Nanaimo has become a regional defence centre I suggest that it is very important that our air terminal facilities be improved. Nanaimo is centrally located on Vancouver island and must have the central emergency air service to take care of any necessary evacuation and emergency flying, as well as mercy and rescue flights.
To ensure the provision of these services I suggest that the Nanaimo airport runway must be lengthened by 1,850 feet and rebuilt to sufficient strength to receive aircraft of a gross weight of 200,000 pounds. Taxiways must be lengthened and strengthened, and a ramp area would have to be constructed in such a manner as to accommodate aircraft of the size of the DC-8, the Boeing 707 or the Vanguard and Britannia. Airport lighting will also require major improvement, and a passenger terminal would have to be built with facilities to accommodate more than 100 persons, but not more than 200 persons. The purchase of fire fighting equipment and airport maintenance equipment would be very expensive. However, such equipment is mandatory for the type of airport envisaged.
I also suggest that negotiations with field suppliers prior to the construction of the ramp area is essential in order to ensure that adequate fuelling facilities are available. Basic radio facilities and navigation facilities would have to be installed-such as I.L.S. and V.O.R. This would also be very expensive. Additional communications and staff facilities would be required in order to provide proper meteorological services and air to ground communications.
An alternate airport for international air services must contain such facilities as accommodation for customs, immigration and health. Nanaimo has less fog than other west coast cities. Airplanes cannot fly into Vancouver at certain times of the year and have to go up to Ashcroft but at Nanaimo we have less fog than Victoria and less than they have at the R.C.A.F. airport at Comox. All of these things should be taken into consideration because today an accident is a terrible thing. You have a loaded jet with over 100

Supply-Transport
people. Someone has to answer for the accidents when they happen. An examination is made to find out who is to blame. In this day and age there is no reason why there should be poor airports on the trans-continental runs.
I urge the Minister of Transport to give this matter serious thought as there is no doubt in my mind that some day the western terminal of trans-continental airlines will be in Vancouver. I made a statement which appeared in the Daily Colonist, back in 1923 that in the near future there would be an air service between Victoria, Seattle and Vancouver. Many who read that statement in the Colonist did not believe it, but, as we know, it has been a fact for some years now. I repeat, I believe that Vancouver island will be the western terminal of Trans-World Air Lines in the future.
I am sure the minister will give these suggestions proper consideration because he is very anxious to do and is doing a very fine job for aviation in Canada and in respect of the many other fields which come under his department. I know he will do what is right. I would certainly like to have the minister out in Nanaimo with me. I could show him just what I have in mind there. I am sure he would agree with me it has more possibilities than any other place on the coast.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on rising to speak on the first item of the estimates of the Minister of Transport I should like to avail myself of this opportunity, on behalf of myself and my constituents and in collaboration with my colleagues, to express my congratulations to the minister in his new portfolio. I have found that I receive very good co-operation from the minister on problems that affect my riding. I feel, judging by the compliments I heard coming from my colleagues, that he will have a long and successful tenure of office in this portfolio.
The subject that brings me to my feet tonight is something that is very serious and affects a great number of my constituents in the northeast area of the constituency of Moose Mountain. I refer to the people who live along and adjacent to the Reston and Wolseley line of the C.P.R. To give the committee a few statistics on it, the construction of the line was commenced in the year 1905. and completed in 1908. The construction was started at Reston and reached Wolseley three years later. The distance was 122.18 miles of rail and 5.68 miles of side track on the division. It paralleled the C.N.R. line for approximately 100 miles, and crossed the line at Maryfield. In 1958, 1,156 carloads of freight originated along the line and 310 carloads were brought into the stations on the line.

Revenue earned in 1958 amounted to $326,757. The southern portion of the line is 85 pound steel and the remainder 56 pound steel. The 85 pound steel was laid only a short time ago.
The problem is this, Mr. Chairman. On December 2, 1959, the C.P.R. made application to the board of transport commissioners to abandon this whole section of line. As I said a moment ago, you can imagine the concern and worry of the people living adjacent to that line when word came through. Immediately upon application by the Canadian Pacific to the board of transport commissioners to abandon that line a meeting was called of the people affected, and the then minister of northern affairs and national resources, now the Minister of Agriculture, and I attended the meeting. A retention committee was set up, chaired by Mr. A. G. Knee-shaw-Mr. Sundstrom was secretary and Mr. Bildfell was treasurer-with members from every municipal administration along the area. They developed a very good brief or representation to make to the board of transport commissioners in their application to oppose the abandonment application. I should like to give the committee a few figures because I think those gentlemen are to be congratulated on the very good job they did in developing this brief. I give this information because I think this problem is pertinent to a lot of other places in western Canada and is of particular interest at this time when we hear recommendations from the Mac-Pherson royal commission on the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National suggesting the necessity of cutting down services on these lines.
The population living along this line is considerable. I should like to give the committee a list of the names of the towns affected. They are as follows: Ewart, Ebor, Maryfield, Fair-light, Walpole, Wawota, Dumas, Kennedy, Bender, Neelby, Windthorst, Baring, Deveron and Adair. Chief among these 14 towns or villages are the towns of Maryfield, Fair-light, Wawota, Kennedy and Windthorst.
In these particular villages and towns are 23 elevators. I mention elevators because years ago in the west when this line was put through it was with the chief idea of transporting livestock and grain which were produced in those rural areas. As a result, the construction of these numerous elevators has been a very important part of the economy of those particular towns. I should like to say to the committee that it is still very important. I was interested in some of the figures compiled by the retention committee. It seems that in the nine year period from 1931 to 1940, the average production of grain at that time was 814,100 bushels. In the 11 year period from 1949 to 1959 the average was

2,280,000 bushels, almost three times as much. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that it is very important to the people living along that line that this fact be considered because we still think there is no other medium besides railways to move efficiently and effectively bulk products such as grain. We do have a road system out there. It is not as modern as some of the roads in the more populated areas. They are gravel roads which are used for the trucking of a certain amount of livestock, but the basic commodity is still grain and it is the basic concern of the people in the area.
Let me give a brief run-down of the population and some of the cost figures. I should like to include some of the figures of the population of the villages and hamlets affected. They are: adults, 617; children, 412; total, 1,029. The population on farms is as follows: adults, 1,326; children, 1,153; total, 2,479, or a grand total of 3,508, who are directly affected, both socially and economically, by the application to remove this line.
I do not think, Mr. Chairman, there would be too much objection to the over-all principle of a cut-back in service on the railroad, but when the application was for the total abandonment of it you can imagine how serious it would be to this portion of the population.
Let me give a resume of the household property. These figures were arrived at by the retention committee through sending out a questionnaire to every householder affected by the railway abandonment. The questionnaire was quite lengthy and interesting. They got a very comprehensive and informative set of figures. The total value of householder property affected is $1,569,470. The amount spent in construction and remodelling since 1940 totals $813,380. The estimated loss if this line were abandoned is $784,645.
In so far as business properties are concerned, I might say that the value of land for privately owned and public buildings including halls, rinks, churches, schools, etc., is $73,066; value of buildings, $1,145,950; value of equipment and stock, $790,868. The total value amounts to $2,009,884. The estimated cost of rehabilitation should this line be abandoned is $411,400.
I have been dealing with the urban area, and I should like now to deal with the rural area. The number of farm units affected is 662. The number of acres of farm land in the affected area amounts to 420,630; the number of acres cultivated, 242,027. There are 480 owners, 120 owners and tenants and 62 tenants in this area. The estimated value of farm land is $8,956,985. The improvements since 1940 amount to $2,252,650. The value
Supply-Transport
of machinery purchased since 1940 is $6,388,994. The total value of all buildings and machinery on farms amounts to $8,641,644.
The area affected is a prosperous mixed farming community. This committee secured figures to indicate the total amount of livestock on this particular land. The livestock total is made up as follows: cattle, 21,124; sheep and swine, 3,341; chickens, 27,390, with a total value of $2,942,340. The total elevator capacity of towns on the line is 1,052,000 bushels. The amount of grain storage required is estimated at 953,500 bushels. The estimated cost of providing this storage is $358,150.
The committee also gathered some statistics concerning what it would cost the municipalities to provide roads in order to assist the farmers in moving their grain by truck should the line be abandoned. The estimated mileage of the new roads necessary is 144 miles. The estimated cost per mile is $3,860. The estimated cost of bridges is $27,900. The estimated loss to buildings and property would be $84,500, for a total of $116,260. The estimated yearly cost of extra road maintenance is $19,442.50 and the estimated yearly loss of taxes, $10,991.04. The total of these two items is $30,433.54.
In so far as the villages affected are concerned, the number of persons who would be put out of work is 33. Since these 33 people are the heads of families, the total number of people involved would be 126. The yearly loss of taxes on railway property would amount to $2,832.99; the yearly loss of taxes on elevator property, $6,749.02; the yearly loss of taxes on other businesses, $2,996.37. The total of these items is $12,578.38 The total estimated loss to municipalities and villages, therefore, would be $159,271.92.
These figures roughly represent urban and rural property, businesses, livestock, machinery and so on with a total value of about $25 million. Then, of course, there would be the social and economic effects on the lives of about 3,500 people. Following these representations to the board of transport commissioners a hearing was held by the board at Moosomin on June 20 of last year and an order was issued by the board on December 12, 1960. This order reads as follows:
In the matter of the application of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, under section 168 of the Railway Act, for an order authorizing the abandonment of its operation between Reston, in the province of Manitoba, and Wolseley, in the province of Saskatchewan, being all of the Reston-Wolseley subdivision, a distance of 122.18 miles:
H. H. Griffin, assistant chief commissioner; J. M. Woodard, commissioner; W. R. Irwin, commissioner; .. .

Supply-Transport
It is hereby ordered as follows:
1.	The Canadian Pacific Railway Company is authorized to abandon operation of its Reston-Wolseley subdivision between Reston, in the province of Manitoba, and Wolseley, in the province of Saskatchewan, a distance of 122.18 miles.
2.	The said abandonment shall not take place earlier than the first day of August, 1961, on not less than ninety days' prior notice forwarded to the municipalities, towns, villages, elevator companies and elevator associations located along the line to be abandoned; a copy of the said notice shall also be filed with the board.
This decision, Mr. Chairman, caused a great deal of surprise and alarm among the people of the area because they felt that the strong representations they made and the statistics they presented concerning the effect of the abandonment on their economy, would have caused the board of transport commissioners to find in favour of their petition. As a result of this finding, the committee had recourse to two alternatives. The first was to apply to the Supreme Court of Canada on the basis of legal technicality, if there were any, existing in the order. Of course, the members of this transport board are qualified gentlemen and there were not any such loopholes in the authorization. The other alternative the committee had was to apply to the governor in council under section 53 of the Railway Act which reads as follows:
The governor in council may at any time, in his discretion, either upon petition of any party, person or company interested, or of his own motion, and without any petition or application, vary or rescind any order, decision, rule or regulation of the board, whether such order or decision is made inter partes or otherwise, and whether such regulation is general or limited in its scope and application; and any order that the governor in council may make with respect thereto is binding upon the board and upon all parties.
I might say that the railway retention committee has taken advantage of the provisions of section 53 of the Railway Act and has made representations to the governor in council to have this order rescinded. I should like to suggest through you, Mr. Chairman, to our good minister that he give every consideration to this application to have the order rescinded. I feel that this should be done on the basis of the following grounds, and I shall mention at least three important factors.
First, I feel that the decision was premature and the board should have awaited the report of the MacPherson royal commission. In the second place, when one compares the evidence and facts presented in connection with this application for the abandonment of the Reston-Wolseley line with several other applications for abandonment made at approximately the same time, one finds glaring inconsistencies in the order authorizing the abandonment of the line. I

feel that this is something that should be looked into. The third point concerns some compromise arrangement. Not too far distant from the Reston-Wolseley line is another line operated by the Canadian National which I mentioned earlier crosses at Mary-field, and I feel that rather than cut out all the services on either one of these lines a compromise arrangement might have been made whereby these two lines would have been merged into a circuit; then the railways might operate one train a week to remove the grain from along the route and the freight from the towns in the affected area.
There is one other point that should be mentioned, namely the economic factors involved in connection with these rural villages and towns if there were a complete abandonment of the line. We all realize that the railroads developed the west and made it known as the breadbasket of the world in the last 50 years.
I might suggest that this is one of the better farming areas in that part of Saskatchewan. It is interesting to note that it has one of the highest concentrations of population in that part of the farming area. It is also interesting to note that it has one of the highest livestock populations per capita of any place in Saskatchewan. In addition, the area is noted for some of the highest quality livestock. This fact was most forcibly brought to my attention a year ago last fall when I was attending the royal winter fair in Toronto. I made inquiries from some of the people in charge of the livestock exhibits there. They told me that 101 head of cattle had been selected from Saskatchewan for exhibition at the royal winter fair. I was greatly interested and proud to note that, out of the 101 head of livestock being exhibited at Toronto, 36 head came from the riding of Moose Mountain. This information indicates the calibre of the livestock raised there and of the people engaged in producing these high quality products.
I feel that the mechants and business people in these towns, particularly the major ones I mentioned, would suffer great hardships both economically and socially, if the line were completely removed and they were forced to sacrifice their businesses, because that is what it would mean. It is extremely hard to remove a business lock, stock and barrel and to find an economic opening somewhere else, as in some neighbouring town. The result is that these people would never be able to overcome the economic loss they would suffer through abandonment of that line.
As I mentioned earlier, the elevator companies affected would also be serious losers

in any move like this. I should like to mention in passing that there are seven different grain companies situated on this line. These are the Manitoba pool, Searle Grain Company, Saskatchewan wheat pool, Parrish and Heim-becker, National Grain Company, Lake of the Woods Company and N. M. Patterson Company. The other 16 elevators out of the 23 elevators I mentioned are made up of the wheat pools, either the Manitoba pool or the Saskatchewan pool, and I think one other town has a National Grain Company elevator.
I think one of the salient features is the fact that, in the handling of agricultural products in the west, grain elevators perform one of the basic functions. Most people from the west will appreciate what I am referring to now. If the line were abandoned completely, it would mean having these elevators demolished at some cost and possibly having them reassembled at other points at a loss or possibly it would mean a complete loss. In addition, abandonment of the line would make it necessary for people living in the rural areas to transport grain over greater distances, as I have pointed out, at greater cost to municipalities trying to provide roads and so on.
On the basis of the foregoing information I most emphatically protest the proposed abandonment of the Reston-Wolseley subdivision of the Canadian Pacific Railway and would ask the minister to give this matter, when it comes to his attention before the governor in council, his very earnest and serious consideration.

Mr. Chairman, at the very outset of my remarks I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) to a problem concerning more particularly the municipality of St. Hubert in my constituency of Chambly-Rouville.
My suspicion that a problem will come up in a year or two arises from an article which I read in the Montreal Gazette of April 19 last, concerning the establishment of a NORAD control centre at St. Hubert airport. No doubt you will allow me to read into the record part of this article in order to point to the nature of the problem and explain it, and above all to indicate the solution which I intend to suggest to the Department of Transport in order to settle it. Here is the article of the Canadian Press which apparently originated in Ottawa:
(Text):
The headquarters of the largest and possibly most vital of the regions through which North American Air Defence Command exercises operational control over combat forces will go underground next year, informed sources said yesterday.
Supply-Transport
The headquarters will be moved from the R.C.A.F. base at St. Hubert, to an underground combat centre at Trout lake near North Bay.
The move is merely awaiting completion of the centre which will house the SAGE-semi-automatic ground environment-electronic system which will control the operations of both manned and unmanned interceptors.
(Translation):
This is not confirmed news, but merely a rumour circulating in military circles and more particularly at army headquarters.
In that case, it seems to me that St. Hubert airport would become a less important military airport and that the number of civilians now working there would probably decrease.
Mr. Chairman, if it is true that such a decision is to be taken by the Department of National Defence, I shall accept the sound reasons advanced for it since this is an important defence problem.
If such a decision were to be arrived at, the government would have the responsibility of using that airport for civilian purposes. If it is decided to remove all the airmen now posted at St. Hubert, the airport will be free and may become a completely civil airport. If they only cut down the military forces, the airport will still be available for civil purposes. I would therefore suggest to the Department of Transport to consider the possibility of making use of the St. Hubert facilities for civil purposes and it is my opinion that this could be done as soon as the authorities of the Department of National Defence decide to move out since there is already some talk about decentralizing the Dorval services. And it will probably be necessary to plan for a civil airport in some other place for test flights or for passenger or freight services.
Mr. Chairman, I offer that suggestion to the Minister of Transport, knowing that he will refer it to the proper person and that he will see to it that his officials study it calmly in order to determine whether it is not possible to reach some practical decision.
I offer that suggestion in quite a selfish intention in my capacity as the member for Chambly-Rouville since the idea is to prevent family wage earners in the St. Hubert, Chambly, St. Bruno, Beloeil and St. Hilaire area from losing their livelihood because of that necessary and warranted decision of the Department of National Defence which could have a serious impact if the government should decide not to make use of that airport.
I know the wisdom of the Conservative government, the Conservative cabinet, and particularly the wisdom of the Minister of Transport and I do not think that there

Supply-Transport
will be any recurrence of what happened under former regimes, according to reports- we will not see any completely abandoned airports that are not used for civilian purposes, when civilian aviation facilities are greatly needed.
Mr. Chairman, may I now examine another problem, namely the problem of passenger transportation from downtown Montreal to Dorval airport. I asked a question to the Minister of Transport in that connection. I asked him if he would forward a suggestion to the railways. I asked him if it would not be possible for the railway companies to provide rail transportation between Dorval and the large hotels and railway stations in downtown Montreal.
I received letters of appreciation in this connection, indicating that such a solution in itself was excellent. There were even some newspaper articles. The next week the Montreal Star published a study of the question. It had to do with questions to the railway companies and the air lines.
The air lines were obviously most favourable, but the railways were reticent. Yet, if the C.P.R. does not want to do anything, the C.N.R. could possibly examine the possibility of such a service.
Allow me, sir, to quote part of an article written by Alfred Ayotte about that matter in La Presse of March 4, 1961-please forgive the personal references, my modesty will suffer-I quote:
The suggestion of the member for Chambly-Rou-ville, Mr. Maurice Johnson, to establish a railway link between the Dorval air terminal and Montreal central station is excellent. We must add that it is excellent in principle, because according to information we have been able to gather, there would be some difficulties in the implementation of such a suggestion. The Minister of Transport, Hon. Mr. Balcer, has passed on to the C.N.R. Mr. Johnson's idea and he has admitted that it has created keen interest among the public.
After what the newspapers have published about the existence of a taxi monopoly at Dorval airport and the inconvenience that resulted for patrons, a railroad would be a relief.
Railway travel offers two advantages: speed and low fares. Would it not be wonderful to leave the plane and get aboard a commuter train to reach downtown Montreal in a short time as it is done in Belgium and as it is probably done in Italy? Indeed, some airports are serviced by trains elsewhere in the world.
A little train takes only twenty minutes to cover the distance between the Brussels airport and the Belgian capital.
After a rapid calculation, I would say that it would take about that time to travel from Dorval to the centre of the city. I will now continue my quotation:
Travellers only have to go down a staircase to reach ground level. In Brussels itself, the trains

reach the station underground. The fare is only the equivalent of 50 cents, in Canadian currency.
Will we be getting the same thing in Montreal? The railroads are non-committal on that point. They are considering the question from a financial point of view and wondering whether a line a few miles long or a few acres of tracks and the inauguration of frequent commuter trains on tracks which are already quite busy, would be profitable.
If they go by the number of passengers in 1960-61, they may well doubt that such a new train service would be profit-making: but if they stopped to consider that in five to ten years from now, the number of passengers will have greatly increased, they would be justified to conclude that the income would justify the expenditure.
In any case, the idea is in the air. It is now up to the railway people and to the Department of Transport to consider the matter and appraise the cost of railway development near the air terminal. If the project could materialize, it would bring about the solution of a ticklish transportation problem.
I would add, Mr. Chairman, that it would perhaps be desirable, when the railway companies change their schedules or their services, either by adding or removing trains, that their decisions be made known to the public. It did happen that railways had some lines in operation on a temporary basis, in anticipation of a special event or that they established new permanent lines without advertising them, in order that the general public might be informed and be able afterwards to use the facilities offered.
As an example, I take the case of the train between Granby and Montreal, when the Canadian National had established a train service in 1959 between those two places, for the duration of the centenary of Granby. Recently, representatives of the Canadian National were complaining of the lack of passengers on that train. It so happened that nobody knew, that publicity was lacking, perhaps as much on the part of the organizations responsible for the centenary celebrations, but certainly on the part of the Canadian National. That is why the service did not have the success desired or hoped for.
Mr. Chairman, I therefore submit this problem to the attention of the minister. I would ask him to put the necessary pressure on the railway companies, in order that they may consider this problem and take a decision, rather than have the matter shelved.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I take the liberty of commenting on a matter which does not come directly under the Minister of Transport. I do not want the minister to think that I am in any way blaming his department or his officials in this regard. However, I should like to deal with this matter just the same,

because it is of general interest and the company involved, the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, must, to a certain extent, be subject to the authority of the board of transport commissioners which comes under the Department of Transport.
Time and time again, in cases of emergency, people have to dial a number to reach someone, without knowing that number. In such cases, they dial the numbers of the Bell Telephone Company information service.
God knows how long the operators take before answering. We have the same thing in the long distance service at night. Of course, I cannot believe it is the operators' fault, unless I am shown evidence to the contrary. It seems to me that their number is much too limited for the requirements of the job. It is time that the company attempt to better that service because, when it applies to the board of transport commissioners for an increase in rates, it will be extremely difficult for the customers to accept any increase.
When the company applied for an increase not so long ago, if I remember correctly, it alleged some extension to or improvement of its services. Since then, I did not notice anything of the kind with regard to information or -long distance services. As I said before, it is certainly not the operator's fault if there are too few of them. It is the company's fault which refuses to employ enough people to ensure good service.
Mr. Chairman, as the voters in Chambly-Rouville know, I am particularly interested in the Richelieu seaway problem. I heard my colleagues make some improvised speeches on the subject. I also heard the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis), earlier this evening, make a statement on that seaway issue. I would like to be able to examine the issue calmly and see what he did say in his speech. The hon. member dealt with the economic soundness of the project. If my memory serves me right, he said that according to various people the project would be economically sound. Now, I shall ask the hon. member, to name those people and authorities because that is precisely the most important point in respect of the Richelieu seaway project.
We cannot but wonder whether, once it is built, that seaway would pay its way. Unfortunately, I did not find any authority or any qualified and competent person having studied the problem who could tell us authoritatively whether the project would be economically sound.
Please note, Mr. Chairman, that I should like to hear someone say so, but I would
Supply-Transport
like to know the people, and be given the references according to whom and which the seaway would be sound, if it were built. That is the most significant point, and because the economic soundness of the project is still unknown, the chamber of commerce of the province of Quebec does not ask this government to undertake the Richelieu seaway project now, alone, or jointly with the government of the United States, without previous consideration.
The Quebec chambers of commerce which are anxious to arouse public interest for this project, dare not maintain that the seaway would be economically sound. What is requested by the chambers of commerce of the province of Quebec and by all the experts who have studied the problem, is that a study be made of the feasibility of the scheme. At the December meeting, which was attended by the member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) and the member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville-whom I did not see before the banquet in the evening- and also by a number of people interested in the scheme, no one among all the experts and among all those who had studied the scheme was able to answer this question of the economic feasibility. I even raised the question with a representative of the port of New York who was giving a talk on the subject. Questions had to be put down in writing, so I wrote my question, and when it came up, the chairman of the panel-it was no doubt a diplomatic gesture-referred the question to a town planner who had been studying the problem. No, I am sorry, he asked the question of another person, a Montreal economist, I think, who came up with some general considerations but would not come out with a definite conclusion.
Though I have been dealing with this matter of economic feasibility, Mr. Chairman, I would not want the voters or rather the people concerned in the Richelieu area, to think I am against the scheme. I merely raise the question in the hope of getting an answer. I suggested last week, as I did in other speeches and in private conversations, that the question be referred to a joint commission including a group of American representatives, or to a strictly Canadian body. After all, we must ask ourselves whether the Richelieu canal, once developed, would be in the best interest of Canada. That is the point.
Mr. Chairman, I am not in any sense antiAmerican. However, I am now reading a book written by an authority in the field, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), and I remember the Americans were not too

Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal briefly with tolls on the Welland ship canal. In 1958 the tolls committee of the St. Lawrence seaway set tolls for the operation of the canal in order to amortize the $29 million in capital costs involved in deepening the canal, over a period of 50 years. This was done on the basis of a 1959 tonnage forecast of 40 million tons, and a 1960 forecast of 43 million tons. During those two years the total tonnage that passed through the canal was 25 million tons below the estimate.
The income forecast for 1959 was $2 million, and the actual income was $1.2 million. The estimated income for 1960 was $2.2 mil-lin, but the actual was $1.3 million. The income was therefore down $1.7 million under the estimate. We find also that the cost of the operation is much higher than the estimate. As a result of this, the net revenues do not meet the operating costs.
I have always taken the position that charging tolls on the Welland canal would in effect toll lock all the ports around lake Ontario, as well as those on the Welland canal. Ships and cargos have free access from lake Erie to the head of the lakes. Ships cannot get out of lake Ontario without paying a toll, and I suggest this is an unjust discrimination against the ports on the shores of lake Ontario.
Most of the plants in Ontario which make use of waterborne traffic are situated on the shores of lake Ontario and the Welland canal. Industry located along the Welland
Supply-Transport
canal when it was toll free. Industry has expanded and developed there on the assumption, and rightly so, that the canal would always be toll free.
The Welland canal was adequate for the purposes for which it was designed before its deepening, and the deepening of the canal did not provide any assistance to the plants to which I have referred. During the first year, its deepening was a hindrance rather than an assistance, because their own canal boats were held up by the slower European boats using the canal. I know of two or three instances when plant boats were held up as long as 12 hours.
Paper companies could not make use of deep draught boats because they obtain their pulpwood down along the St. Lawrence and around the shores of lake Superior, in areas that did not have deep harbours for loading. They therefore must use shallow draught boats.
There have been rumours in the area of the Welland ship canal that the canal is going to be twin locked. New industry will not settle there, nor will the industries which are there enlarge, because of the uncertainty of the policy of the government in this connection. I say this is uncertain, because of the fact that if new locks were built, and the cost was amortized over a period of over 40 or 50 years, the position of the plants along that canal would be economically untenable.
The tolls on the Welland canal were imposed, as I have said, in an attempt to amortize the original cost of deepening over 50 years as well as to pay operating costs.
At the present time the United States is spending $150 million to deepen the channels in the Detroit river, the St. Clair river and St. Mary river. I have seen references in the press two or three times reporting that the Americans have said they have the right to recover tolls in connection with the deepening of that part of their waterway if we collect tolls because of the deepening of the Welland canal.
I may say also that industries situated near the locks at Sault Ste. Marie have access to their properties without paying any toll. I think it is only right that industries along the Welland canal should have the same privilege.
The tolls structure was to be examined in five years. This would be in the fall of 1963. It strikes me that the capital cost, including the deficits, might easily be somewhere between $35 million and $40 million instead of the estimated $29 million. Therefore, at that time we would need to amortize the $35 million to $40 million over 45 years instead of

Supply-Transport
the $29 million over 50 years. To my mind that would put up the tolls even if we did not have any twinning of the locks. This creates uncertainty in the minds of people in the industries in that area. They have two uncertainties, one because of the deficits, and the other because of their fear of twinning of those locks. If the locks are twinned and they are charged for it in tolls it certainly will be disastrous for their industries. I would say that industries in my part of the country look at this matter with some concern. I should like to hear the minister pass some comment on it.

I had almost given up hope that I would get on tonight. I am always glad to take the adjournment.
I covered a certain amount of the subject matter in connection with the Canadian National Railways when I spoke last but there are one or two things that I should like to clear up. The hon. member for Vancouver East touched on the matter of passenger service and dealt particularly with reservations. Without repeating what he said I can verify or corroborate everything that he said in regard to the matter of reservations and of having to wait and when you get to the train you find space had not been all booked up as you had been told. But the part that impresses me very much-and I think most hon. members have come to the same conclusion-is that the directors, whether it is the head of the board of directors or others, have come to the conclusion that they should try to fold up the passenger service in this country because it is not a paying proposition. Therefore, they are going to do their best to get rid of it. It is not a very easy thing to do because the minute a passenger line is slated for cancellation of course the members in that particular area are seized upon by their constituents and are asked to see that something is done about it through bringing it to the attention of the Minister of Transport.
Hon. members have been congratulating the minister all night. Probably the minister deserves our sympathy and condolences in his holding of this position because generally he is the whipping boy. He has to take the whip lash of every person in this house who has a grievance from his constituents, or from a person who was laid off by the railway. They come to the house and they confront him with the situation and he has to tell them that he will take it up with the president or the chairman of the board of directors. Then he comes back with the story that they have done their best but they could not avoid laying them off. They have to give them all a chance. This is what the Minister of Transport has to go through. It is not

only this minister but the previous minister. They all go through the very same thing. The pattern is the same. They have to go off and come back with a story which alleviates the situation. Peace reigns until the next time someone is laid off. The whole sum and substance of the problem is that the railway passenger service is not paying and the managers of the railway have to fold it up.
What I say is that if the passenger service is not paying, then the wisest thing to do is to terminate it. But if the railroads are going to continue it, then they should give service. It is no use running a service that is down at the heels and is on a hodge-podge basis. If they are going to give service they should give the very best service there is. I do not think they are even trying to do that. If they were trying to give service, then they would have the trains running on time and they would be giving of their best; they would be giving what could be called a high-class service.
I have spoken time after time in the house and tried to depict what took place at the Ottawa station and also at the Toronto station. Whenever I ran into what I called shabby or sloppy service I would bring it up. When I first started I tried to put a little humour into it and depict it as I saw it. I tried to make sure I was not being too severe, but what I did was just entertain hon. members, and they thought it was nothing more than good humour. But when I started to comment upon the board of directors who I thought should do something about it, well, then, I saw there was a little change. They did attempt to do something about the situation in Ottawa; but surely they did not have to wait for 20 years to try to do something about improving the service in Ottawa. I will say this for them. They have taken the trouble to so bring in the trains as to make it easier for the people to get off the trains and come to the station. They now do not have to walk so far. The reason why I took this attitude was that I had seen some passengers who could hardly walk; they were lame or handicapped, and there was no service to help them carry their grips. Some of the people were obviously infirm or had heart conditions. They were subject to the inconvenience of having to walk a long distance.
Then I checked into the way in which the freight and also the baggage were handled, in the stations. I do not blame men for trying to earn their living; they are doing what they are told. They took the baggage from the express and they put it on a lorry. What did they do with it? They ran it over to No. 3 bay and put it on another car, waiting there,

instead of taking a truck or a car as it comes in to the bay and then transferring it over to another vehicle. That would save a lot of time and not inconvenience the passengers or the people in the station. One fellow said to me, "Why do they not do it this way?" I looked at him and said, "My dear friend, do you not understand why they do not do it that way? It is quite obvious they do not do it that way because it is the simple and proper way. That is why they are not doing it that way".
